conclusion.justification: The report explicitly concludes that the claim is not supported by the strongest evidence, citing major expert reviews and prospective studies showing that induced abortion does not cause an increased risk of breast cancer.
conclusion.label: rejects

report:
**Conclusion:** The claim is not supported by the strongest available evidence. Major expert reviews conclude that induced abortion does **not** cause an increased risk of breast cancer.

Why some people believe there is a link: earlier case–control studies sometimes reported higher rates of prior abortion among people with breast cancer. But these designs can be vulnerable to reporting/recall bias—e.g., cases and controls may differ in whether they disclose a prior abortion. A large collaborative reanalysis found retrospective abortion reporting produced misleading results, plausibly for that reason.

More reliable prospective studies collect abortion information before a breast-cancer diagnosis. In the 2004 collaborative analysis, the relative risk in studies with prospective information was 0.93 for induced abortion (a value below 1, and not evidence of increased risk). A 2015 systematic review/meta-analysis of prospective studies likewise concluded that the evidence was insufficient to support a positive association.

This interpretation is also the position of the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists: early research was inconsistent and methodologically difficult, whereas more rigorous later studies showed no causal relationship. The National Cancer Institute convened a 2003 expert workshop to review population, clinical, and animal evidence on reproductive events and breast-cancer risk.

Sources:  
- https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0140673604158352  
- https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10552-015-0536-1  
- https://www.acog.org/clinical/clinical-guidance/committee-opinion/articles/2009/06/induced-abortion-and-breast-cancer-risk
